pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** Power of Eruptions

- **Standards — UK (DfE, England):** Not a KS1 science topic; eruptions and their effects sit in the **KS2 Geography** programme ('volcanoes and earthquakes', ages 7–11). At 5–7 teach as enrichment supported by KS1 'Working scientifically' (observing and comparing using pictures/sources).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No K–2 PE names eruptions directly; the anchor is **2-ESS1-1** (Earth events occur quickly or slowly) — an eruption is the canonical fast, landscape-changing event. CCC [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1, 2-ESS2-1].' Foreshadows grade-4 ESS2 (surface processes reshape the land).

- **Operational details:** This is an APPRECIATION topic — the aim is for children to grasp that an eruption is a powerful, dramatic event that can reshape the land around it. The evidence is picture-driven: compare the landscape BEFORE and AFTER an eruption (a green valley becomes an ash-covered plain; new lava rock forms; a cone grows taller; a new island appears). Use real before/after imagery. Pitch the tone as awe, not terror — pair 'powerful and dangerous' with the reassuring, true idea that eruptions can also BUILD land and volcanic soil later becomes very fertile, so life returns. Keep specific case studies (Pompeii, named eruptions) and eruption TYPES for the 7–9 topics; here, appreciate the power and see the change.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can call an eruption powerful/dramatic and point to how it changed an area using before/after pictures; they are NOT expected to explain eruption mechanisms or classify eruption types. Manage the affective side — build awe, not fear — and correct 'an eruption destroys everything forever / nothing ever grows back'.
bestPractices: Use real before/after imagery so the landscape change is evidence-based, matching the 'compare using pictures' objective
Let children CAUSE the change (press to erupt) so the power is felt, then compare before/after
Pitch for awe, not terror — pair 'powerful/dangerous' with the true reassurance that land recovers and volcanic soil is fertile
Name concrete changes an eruption makes (new lava rock, ash cover, taller cone, new island) rather than vague 'destruction'
Defer named case studies (Pompeii) and eruption types to the 7–9 topics; keep this to appreciating power and change
Build on 'What Is a Volcano' — assume children can name a volcano and lava before appreciating an eruption's power
keyRepresentations: Before/after landscape pair (green valley → ash-covered plain with new lava rock)
A press-to-erupt scene that reshapes the land (lava, ash, growing cone)
'And later…' time step showing plants returning on fertile ash
Real photographs of eruptions and their aftermath
commonMisconceptions: 'An eruption destroys everything forever and nothing grows back' — land recovers; weathered ash makes very fertile soil
'Eruptions only destroy' — they also BUILD land, new rock, taller mountains and even new islands
'Lava is the only thing an eruption does' — ash, new landforms and changed terrain are also part of the power (kept simple here)
'Every eruption is a giant explosion' — eruptions vary in power (types come later); here just appreciate they can be dramatic
'The changed land stays lifeless' — plants and animals return over time

learn.summary: Help 5–7 year olds appreciate that a volcanic eruption is a powerful, dramatic event that reshapes the land around a volcano, and that over time life returns, helped by volcanic ash that slowly breaks down into fertile soil. The core evidence is comparing the landscape before and after an eruption using pictures. Aim for awe, not fear: an eruption changes the land, it does not ruin it forever. Keep named case studies (e.g. Pompeii) and eruption types for older topics. Assume children can already name a volcano and lava.

activities.title: Press to erupt, then compare before and after
feedback: If a child says 'nothing changed', flip back and forth on the toggle and point to a specific hotspot: the green valley is now covered in grey ash with new black rock — that is a big change.
If a child thinks the land stays lifeless, move the 'and later…' slider forward and point to the green shoots: weathered ash makes rich soil, so plants come back.
If a child thinks the eruption is a tiny dribble, replay the eruption and note the scale: lava spreads across the whole valley and ash covers the fields.
Affirm awe: 'Yes — it is powerful AND the land can recover. Both are true.'
activities.rationale: The target evidence is comparing the landscape before and after an eruption using pictures, and the concept is the drama of transformation. Letting the child cause the change and then toggle between states makes 'powerful and land-changing' felt and directly comparable, and the time step attaches the reassuring recovery idea to the same scene. Causing the change and the live before/after toggle are offered as concrete mechanisms, not as the only way to teach this.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-ESS1-1 frames a volcanic eruption as a quick Earth event that changes the surface; CCC 'Things may change slowly or rapidly'
Eruptions reshape the landscape (new lava rock, ash cover, new cones/islands) and weathered volcanic ash later forms very fertile soil so vegetation returns
learnerActions: Look at a calm scene: a green valley with a quiet mountain. Say what you see.
Press an 'erupt' trigger and watch what happens: lava pours out and cools into new black rock, ash drifts down and blankets the fields, and the cone grows taller.
Flip a before/after toggle (or drag a reveal across the scene) to switch between the original land and the changed land.
Tap 'what changed?' hotspots and name each difference out loud: new black rock, ash cover, and a taller cone.
Advance a gentle time slider labelled 'and later…' and watch green shoots push up through the ash.
Answer aloud: 'Did the land grow back? Why do plants grow well here now?'
activities.intendedInsight: An eruption is powerful and can completely change the landscape; the land is reshaped and covered, but over time plants return and the volcanic soil is very fertile — so an eruption both reshapes and renews the land.

activities.title: Before / after / later picture pairs with tap-to-reveal
feedback: If a child only names ash, point to the changed outline: the hill is a different shape and there is new rock — and, if the pictures show it, a valley has been filled or a river has been pushed to a new path — the land itself changed, not just a mess on top.
If a child thinks the land stays black and dead, open the 'later' picture: green plants grow because the ash soil is rich.
Praise accurate comparisons: 'You found a real change between the two pictures.'
activities.rationale: Still before/after/later pairs map directly onto the picture-based evidence and reliably deliver the comparison. A still pair conveys the change clearly but does not convey the felt power of the event happening, so it works well as a lower-cost route or a follow-up to the interactive eruption. Real photographs keep the comparison evidence-based.
sourceClaims: Eruptions reshape the landscape (new lava rock, ash cover, new cones/islands) and weathered volcanic ash later forms very fertile soil so vegetation returns
learnerActions: Study a paired illustration or real photographs: a green valley, then the same place as an ash-covered plain with new lava rock.
Tap points on the 'after' picture and name each change (ash cover, black lava rock, changed hill shape).
Lift an 'and later…' flap (or tap a third 'years later' picture) to see plants returning on the fertile ash.
Say in your own words how the land is different and what came back.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing before and after pictures shows that an eruption changes the shape and surface of the land, and a later picture shows that life returns over time.

activities.title: Eyewitness account: the valley before and the morning after
feedback: If a child stays fearful, have the character emphasise recovery: 'It was powerful, and the fields grew green again.'
If a child forgets the change, ask them to name one difference between 'before' and 'the morning after'.
activities.rationale: An in-role account can convey drama and reassurance vividly and support the affective goal of awe over fear. It is offered as a complement: at 5–7 the most reliable route to appreciating the change is still seeing the before/after imagery, so pair the spoken account with pictures rather than relying on words alone.
learnerActions: Listen to a friendly character describe what the valley looked like before the eruption, and what it looked like the morning after.
Ask the character your own question, for example 'Did it grow back?'
Listen to the reassuring, true answer that plants return over time on the rich ash soil, and retell one thing that changed and one thing that came back.
activities.intendedInsight: An eruption is a dramatic event that changed the place the character describes, and the land recovers over time — so the feeling is awe, not terror.

activities.title: Check: match before to after and spot what changed
feedback: If a child picks 'nothing changed', show the paired pictures again and name a concrete change.
If a child thinks the land stays dead, point to the 'plants return' option and explain the fertile-ash reason.
activities.rationale: A matching/selected-response check can confirm that a child recognises the before/after change and the recovery idea. Recognition-only tasks confirm identification but do not by themselves build the appreciation or awe that is the point of this topic, so use this as a check after the experiential activities, not as the main teaching.
learnerActions: Match each 'before' landscape to its correct 'after' landscape.
Answer: 'How did the eruption change the land?' and reject a 'nothing changed' option by explaining what actually changed.
Answer: 'What happens to the land years later?' choosing the option where plants return.
activities.intendedInsight: I can identify that an eruption changes the land and that life returns later, distinguishing real change from 'nothing happened'.

constraints: This is an appreciation/conceptual topic for ages 5–7: children should be able to call an eruption powerful/dramatic and point to how it changed an area using before/after pictures. They are NOT expected to explain eruption mechanisms or classify eruption types.

Manage the affective side: build awe, not fear. Always pair 'powerful and dangerous' with the true reassurance that, over time, the land recovers and life returns, helped by volcanic ash that breaks down into fertile soil.
Defer named case studies (e.g. Pompeii) and eruption TYPES to the 7–9 topics.

Name concrete changes (new lava rock, ash cover, a changed cone shape — often taller, but sometimes lower if part of the mountain is blasted away — filled/reshaped valleys, a diverted river, and — only for coastal/sea scenes — a new island) rather than vague 'destruction'. Do not place a 'new island' change in a landlocked valley scene.
Build on prior 'What Is a Volcano' learning: assume children can name a volcano and lava before appreciating an eruption's power.
Use real before/after imagery where possible so the landscape change is evidence-based.

Still-picture pairs and the eyewitness account are scaffolds for the felt power of the event; the interactive 'cause the change' scene conveys the drama more directly but a still pair still teaches the change effectively.
Recognition/matching checks confirm identification but do not elicit the independent appreciation that is the teaching goal.
Correct the misconception that an eruption destroys everything forever, and the opposite underestimation that eruptions are gentle dribbles.

Standards context: not a KS1 science topic in England (eruptions sit in KS2 Geography, ages 7–11); at 5–7 teach as enrichment via KS1 'Working scientifically' (observing/comparing with pictures). US anchor is NGSS 2-ESS1-1 (fast Earth events).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked verified:false in the original row (the fertile-ash/landscape-reshaping claim and the England KS2 Geography placement). The fertile-soil and recovery claim is central to the awe-not-fear framing and to several activities; treat it as a reasonable general volcanology statement pending verification.

Recovery timescales and the degree to which plants return vary by eruption, climate, and location; the 'and later… plants return' step is a simplification appropriate for this age, not a universal guarantee for every site or timeframe.

The original did not establish comparative efficacy or necessity of any single medium; claims that only a press-to-erupt interactive conveys the power, or that 3D 'adds nothing', have been softened to scoped affordances rather than universal laws.

'New island appears' is only coherent for a coastal/sea before-after pair; it must NOT be named as a change in the landlocked green-valley scene. Confirm any imagery used actually depicts island-building before presenting it as the demonstrated change.

probeDeeper: Look at these two pictures — before the eruption and many years after. What's different? What came back?
Why might plants grow really well in the soil near an old volcano?
Does the eruption change the shape of the land, or just cover it? How can you tell?
Is an eruption only bad for the land, or can something good come from it too?
assess.correctAnswer: The friend is wrong. An eruption is powerful and dramatically changes the land — burying and reshaping the area — but over time plants grow back, often very well, because volcanic ash makes the soil rich. The land is changed, not ruined forever.

errorPatterns.pattern: An eruption only destroys — the land is dead and ruined forever
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show before / just-after / years-later pictures; ash enriches the soil and plants return.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the land is ruined forever and nothing grows back.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says nothing grows back and the land stays black forever.

errorPatterns.pattern: An eruption just makes a mess on top — it doesn't change the shape of the land
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare before/after — eruptions build new land, fill valleys, and can move rivers.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — the eruption just makes a mess but the land stays the same shape.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies the landscape itself changes (new hills, filled valleys, new rock).

errorPatterns.pattern: Eruptions are gentle little dribbles (underestimates the power)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show real eruption photos/footage to convey the scale and power.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes eruptions as small or harmless.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks an eruption only destroys and the land is dead forever, or doesn't see it as powerful or land-changing.
responseLevels.full: Explains an eruption is a powerful event that reshapes the land AND that life returns over time (rich ash soil), comparing before/after/later — change, not permanent ruin.
responseLevels.partial: Describes the eruption as powerful and destructive but doesn't recognise that the land is reshaped or that life returns over time.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: After a volcano erupts and covers the land in ash and lava, everything nearby is buried and black. A friend says, 'That land is ruined forever — nothing will ever grow there again.' Do you agree? What happens to the land around a volcano after an eruption?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can describe an eruption as powerful and dramatic (first tier) yet believe the change is only destruction. Asking what happens AFTERWARD, over time, separates 'it only destroys, forever' from 'it reshapes the land, and life returns'.
